# Preface {.unnumbered}

This is a practical, opinionated guide to getting real work done on **MedicineBow**,
the University of Wyoming's flagship high-performance computing (HPC) cluster, run by
the **Advanced Research Computing Center (ARCC)**.

It is written for people joining the **ASCEND** engine and its **ARID** program —
researchers doing wildfire, fire-weather, atmospheric, and geospatial modeling — but
almost everything here applies to any new MedicineBow user. It assumes you are
comfortable-ish on a computer but have never used a shared supercomputer before. Every
chapter tries to explain *why* before *how*, because on a cluster the "why" is usually
what keeps you out of trouble.

## Why this book exists

MedicineBow is a genuinely large, shared machine, and the official documentation — the
[ARCC wiki](https://pages.arcc.uwyo.edu/arcc-wiki/main/) — is good but has gaps and,
in a few places, is out of date relative to the machine as it actually runs today. The
content here was written by working through onboarding on the live cluster and
**cross-checking every important claim against the running system** in July 2026. Where
the docs and the machine disagree, this book follows the machine and calls out the
conflict, because a newcomer following stale docs will hit exactly those conflicts.

::: {.callout-note}
## This is not an official ARCC document
It's a community onboarding guide. It can drift out of date, and ARCC can change
policy at any time. When in doubt, the
[official wiki](https://pages.arcc.uwyo.edu/arcc-wiki/main/) and
`arcc-help@uwyo.edu` are authoritative. Corrections are very welcome.
:::

## The shortest possible orientation

If you read nothing else, read this:

1. **You cannot request your own account — your PI must.** No project, no account.
   (See @sec-account.)
2. **Nothing on the cluster is backed up.** Not home, not project, not scratch. There
   are snapshots, but they live on the same array. (See @sec-storage.)
3. **Never run real computation on a login node.** Log in, then hand work to the
   scheduler (Slurm) or grab an interactive session. (See @sec-why-scheduler.)
4. **Every job must name your project account** with `--account=<project>` — it's the
   one directive you cannot omit. (See @sec-anatomy.)
5. **The partition and QOS you choose decide how long you wait and how big you can go.**
   Short test runs and long simulations belong in different queues. This is the point of
   @sec-partitions and @sec-queue-times, and it's the single most useful thing to get
   right early.

## How the book is organized

- **Part I** gets you an account and logged in.
- **Part II** is a minimal Linux survival kit — no more than you need.
- **Part III** covers the filesystems and moving data in and out.
- **Part IV** covers software: modules, conda, and containers.
- **Part V** is the heart of the book: **Slurm**, the batch scheduler — how to ask for
  resources, pick a queue, watch your jobs, run arrays, use GPUs, and survive
  preemption and failures.
- **Part VI** is quick reference: a cheat sheet, troubleshooting, and a glossary.

Conventions: shell commands you type are shown in `code blocks`. Boxes marked
**Gotcha** or **Important** are places people reliably get burned — they earned their
place by actually biting someone.

Let's get you an account.
